summary: Describes the syslog protocol used to carry event notification messages. It uses a layered design that allows different transports, and defines a message format with structured vendor extensions. This is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3164.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5424 defines a common format for syslog event messages and separates that format from the transport used to deliver them. This lets syslog features use different transports without redefining the message each time.

questions: what is the syslog message format
how is the syslog priority value calculated
what is structured data in syslog
subtitle: A layered, extensible message format for sending event notifications to syslog collectors.

tldr.problem: Syslog extensions lacked a transport-independent message standard, so separate extensions risked defining incompatible message formats and delivery methods.
tldr.mechanism: The protocol separates syslog content, application behavior and transport. A message has a priority and identifying header, optional structured data and an optional free-form message; TLS transport support is required.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5424 provides a common foundation for syslog extensions and obsoletes RFC 3164. It does not define message storage or a transport protocol itself.

today: RFC 5424 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2009. It obsoletes RFC 3164, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why Syslog Has a Layered Standard
sections.content:
Syslog carries event notifications. Earlier work on reliable and secure syslog extensions lacked a Standards-Track specification independent of any transport. Without a shared format, each extension could define its own packet and transport, creating compatibility problems.

RFC 5424 separates message content from transport and defines a standard message format that extensions can build on. It does not specify how messages are stored. Its predecessor, RFC 3164, described implementations observed in the field.
sections.plainLanguage: Syslog features need one message format that does not depend on how messages travel. This RFC defines that format and leaves storage outside the protocol.

sections.title: Syslog Layers and Roles
sections.content:
Syslog has three layers: content, application and transport. Content is the management information in a message. The application layer generates, interprets, routes and stores messages. The transport layer sends messages and receives them.

An originator creates content, a collector gathers it for analysis, and a relay forwards messages between originators, relays and collectors. The protocol does not acknowledge message delivery. Originators and relays may send copies to more than one destination, and these roles may share a system.
sections.plainLanguage: The format separates the event information from the software that handles it and the transport that carries it. A message can pass through relays before a collector receives it.

sections.title: Transport Mappings
sections.content:
RFC 5424 defines no transport protocol. Implementations must support a TLS-based transport mapping and should also support UDP. Deployments are recommended to use TLS. A transport must not deliberately change a syslog message; any temporary change at the sender must be reversed at the receiver.

Message-size support is determined by the transport mapping. Every transport receiver must accept messages up to 480 octets and should accept messages up to 2048 octets. A receiver may truncate an oversized message at the end or discard it.
sections.plainLanguage: The message format can be carried over different transports, but TLS support is required. A transport must deliver the message unchanged, and its rules define the size limits.

sections.title: The Header and Priority Value
sections.content:
A syslog message consists of a HEADER, a space, STRUCTURED-DATA and, optionally, a space and MSG. The header contains PRI, VERSION, TIMESTAMP, HOSTNAME, APP-NAME, PROCID and MSGID. Header fields use seven-bit ASCII; a hyphen is the NILVALUE for a missing value.

PRI combines Facility and Severity. Its numeric value is Facility multiplied by 8 plus Severity. Facility values range from 0 through 23, and Severity values from 0 through 7. VERSION is 1 in this specification. TIMESTAMP follows a restricted form of RFC 3339: T is required and uppercase, Z is uppercase, leap seconds are forbidden, and fractional seconds contain no more than 6 digits.

HOSTNAME identifies the originator, with a fully qualified domain name preferred when available. APP-NAME and MSGID support filtering. PROCID has no interoperable meaning, but a changed value can indicate a break in syslog reporting.
sections.plainLanguage: The header tells a collector the priority, time and source of an event. PRI combines a facility and severity, while a hyphen marks a field with no value.

sections.title: Structured Data and Extensions
sections.content:
STRUCTURED-DATA holds zero or more parseable elements. With no elements it must contain the NILVALUE. An element has an SD-ID and zero or more name-value parameters in brackets. Names without an at-sign are assigned through IETF review; an organization can define private names using a name followed by its private enterprise number.

Parameter values use UTF-8. A double quote, backslash and closing bracket must be escaped. The same SD-ID must not occur more than once in a message. Once an SD-ID or parameter's meaning is defined, it must not be changed; a new name is needed for a change. The RFC defines optional elements for timestamp quality, origin information and message metadata.

MSG is free-form event text. UTF-8 messages begin with the UTF-8 byte order mark and use the shortest form. Structured data and message text can contain control characters, so receivers must handle them carefully.
sections.plainLanguage: Structured data adds labeled values that software can parse without guessing. Organizations can use private names, while registered names keep the same meaning once defined.

sections.title: Security, Delivery and Congestion
sections.content:
The message format does not provide confidentiality, integrity, replay detection or guaranteed delivery. Attackers may observe messages, alter them, replay old messages or discard them. The RFC recommends secure transport and notes that signatures could help prevent changes to timestamps used in replay attacks.

UDP lacks congestion control, which is one reason TLS support is required and TLS is recommended for deployments. If a sender must drop queued messages, the RFC recommends dropping lower-severity messages before higher-severity ones. Operators should also prevent forwarding loops, protect collectors from excessive or false messages and ensure that log traffic does not overwhelm network links.

UTF-8 and control characters can create misleading or unreadable log entries. Receivers should handle NUL and other controls carefully, and truncated messages may lose important information; the RFC advises placing important data early.
sections.plainLanguage: Syslog messages are not automatically private, authenticated or protected from replay. A secure transport, careful handling of log text and sensible traffic limits reduce these risks.

viz.caption: THE MAIN FIELDS IN A SYSLOG HEADER

items.title: PRI
items.text: Facility and Severity combined into one priority value.

items.title: TIMESTAMP
items.text: Time when the message was created, or NILVALUE.

items.title: HOSTNAME and APP-NAME
items.text: Identify the originating host and application.

items.title: PROCID and MSGID
items.text: Help distinguish a reporting process and event type.
